source.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Localized Feature Editing with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Yu-Hu Shang; Xiang Cheng; Dian-Yun Wang; Yimeng Ren; Xue-Xiong Luo; Hang Yang; Hui-Jia Wu; Zhao-Feng He

record.tranche_reason: The study empirically examines SAE-recovered features in LLMs and reports feature-level measurements and interventions relevant to V4, using methods different from the original toy-model work.
record.gate_note: The toxicity and fluency effects of manipulating the top-5 toxicity-related SAE features (Figure 1), and the SAE-feature toxicity-detection analysis (Figure 4), bear on V4. Overall DeLFE detoxification results, ablations of DeLFE components, and efficiency results are outcomes of the paper's proposed method, not additional tests of the listed representation claims. Feature-selection statistics used to choose the features are not results rows.
record.test_reason: This is a detoxification-method paper. It uses pretrained SAEs (Gemma Scope, SAE Lens) as a tool and reports its own method's performance. The polysemanticity of neurons is asserted from citations, not measured. The Figure 1 motivating study is a steering effect on toxicity, not a measure of superposition or of feature recovery. The Figure 4 heatmaps are a qualitative class-separability comparison inside the method's own pipeline, with no measure of how features are spread across neurons or how well the SAE recovers them. No version of the claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The main conclusion is that DeLFE, which learns a toxicity subspace over selected SAE features and applies a flow-matching transformation, outperforms 12 baselines on detoxification across Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B and Mistral-7B while keeping fluency and MMLU performance. The finding that indiscriminate SAE-feature ablation harms fluency is the motivation, not the conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a toy-model superposition experiment. It uses pretrained SAEs, toxicity labels, feature selection, toxicity-subspace learning, and flow-matching transformations to detoxify LLMs.

fits_no_version.finding: On RTP-Extreme, scaling up the top-5 toxicity SAE features increases toxic output. Ablating them cuts toxic outputs by 76.4% but more than doubles fluency degradation on non-toxic generations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering individual SAE features in LLMs causally controls a target attribute (toxicity), with collateral quality costs.

fits_no_version.finding: On Gemma-2-2B layer 20, stable-selected SAE features show clearer toxic versus non-toxic activation differences than raw activations. The evidence is qualitative (Figure 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features give more linearly separable attribute representations than raw residual activations.

record.problems: For the Figure 1 interventions, the model and numerical baseline are not stated in the text. Figure 4's recall and F1 values are only presented in the figure, without numerical values transcribed in the text. The feature evidence concerns toxicity-related features and does not establish general SAE feature completeness or stability.
record.rows_left_out: Overall DeLFE results in Table 1 and subsequent method evaluations are not included because they measure the proposed detoxification method's performance rather than the representation claims. Figure 4's toxicity-subspace classifier result is also not separately rowed: the claim-relevant result is the SAE-feature representation comparison recorded in r4.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, geometry, or sparsity transition.
All: polysemanticity is only asserted from citations.
No measure of feature distribution across neurons or of SAE recovery quality. Pretrained SAEs are used as given.
No completeness, stability or canonicality tests.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and the V4 labels are overturned. The SAE is a tool here, and the paper's feature-level results serve its own detoxification method. Table 1, Figure 3, Table 2 and the MMLU results are method performance and were correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study examines toxicity-related features in its tested model/settings; it does not establish how broadly features are distributed across neurons or how generally SAE recovery works across LLMs.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features as the model's units.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Scaled up activations of the top-5 toxicity-related SAE features.
rows.value: Scaling up toxic feature activations markedly increases the generation of toxic content.
rows.note: The text does not identify the model or give a numerical value for this intervention.
rows.check: This measures the toxicity effect of steering SAE features. It does not show that features are spread across neurons or that sparse features are recovered. The model and baseline are not stated, and the value is figure-only or qualitative.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Ablated activations of the top-5 toxicity-related SAE features and reconstructed model activations.
rows.note: The paper also describes toxicity mitigation from ablating these activations.
rows.check: The 76.4% toxicity reduction from ablating SAE features is a steering or mitigation outcome, not evidence on V4. The model and baseline are not stated.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Ablated activations of the top-5 toxicity-related SAE features and reconstructed model activations.
rows.value: More than a twofold increase in fluency degradation.
rows.note: This reports a cost of indiscriminate feature ablation; the numerical fluency measure is not stated here.
rows.check: The fluency cost of ablation is an intervention side effect, unrelated to any version. 'partial' was not a meaningful state for V4 here.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured toxicity-classification recall and F1 using SAE features after stable feature selection; compared representations with raw activations.
rows.measure: Recall and F1 for toxicity detection; SAE features show sparse dimensions with clear class-specific activation differences and enhance class separability relative to raw activations.
rows.baseline: Raw activations; numerical baseline values are figure only.
rows.value: Figure only; the text states that stable-selected SAE features reveal sparse dimensions with clear class-specific activation differences.
rows.note: The paper says Figure 4 reports recall and F1 but the values are not available in the text. The authors describe the SAE representation as more class-separable than raw activations.
rows.check: This is a qualitative heatmap of 256 features chosen by the method's own t-statistic selection on Gemma-2-2B layer 20. Separability is versus raw activations, with no numbers in the text. It is an evaluation of a method component, not a test of whether SAEs recover the model's features.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Toxicity-related SAE features in the reported LLM experiments
reader_labels.reason: The SAE representation shows sparse, class-specific toxicity activation patterns, and manipulating selected SAE features changes toxicity as described (r1, r2, r4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Indiscriminate ablation on originally non-toxic generations
reader_labels.reason: Ablation is reported to cause more than a twofold increase in fluency degradation for originally non-toxic generations, qualifying the utility of feature-level intervention (r3).
